title: Kalki, the one still to come
hookLine: one name in Vishnu's series is still written as will be
carry: god's coming isn't finished: kalki will be
tomorrow: the Bhagavata forecasts Kalki's age. why does it sound like today?
last: TEN IS A FRAME, NOT A FENCE.

cards: Weather apps, countdowns to graduation, a tracking number that says out for delivery: a lot of life is lived toward something that hasn't happened yet.
Read the Bhagavata's verses on Vishnu's forms and the grammar runs in the past. The fish came. Rama came.
Krishna came, and left. Then the last name, and the verbs change. He will be born.
He will ride. He will set things right. One name in the whole series is still written as will be, and it's Kalki.

teach.b: At the twilight of the age, when those who rule have become little better than robbers, the Lord will be born as Kalki, in the village of Shambhala, in the house of a Brahmin named Vishnuyasha.
He'll mount a swift horse named Devadatta, sword in hand, ride across the earth, and put down the robbers who rule as kings.
Behind it stands Krishna's promise in the Gita: whenever dharma falls, I come, age after age.

teach.h: ONE READING: STILL AHEAD. ANOTHER: THE AGE HAS AN END.
teach.b: Kalki is that promise with its last line still ahead. Readers hold this in more than one way, so let two of them speak. One reads it straight: this is an event still ahead.

The Purana says will be, and it gives a village, a father's name, a horse's name. Texts that name the horse, this reader says, aren't speaking in riddles, and waiting for Kalki is part of living in this age.
Another reader listens for what the promise does right now.

The dark age already has a name waiting at its close, so the dark isn't the last word. On this reading, Kalki is the age's horizon, and the point is the hope more than the date. Notice what the two share.

Neither throws the verses away. Both hear the list of descents as open, its last line still unwritten. Where they part is whether the horse is coming down a road, or standing at the edge of every hard day.

how: Hindus hold the Kalki verses in more than one way: some speak of Kalki as still to come, and others read the promise as a sign that the dark age has an end.

o: the village where the last age of the world begins
the horse a god will ride at the end of the age
the form of Vishnu still to come, on a swift horse

games.q: the one still to come — tap the pairs.
p: the Brahmin in whose house he's born

s: every form in the series is told in the past tense
Kalki is written as will be: he will be born, he will ride.
the Bhagavata says Kalki's horse is white
these verses name the horse, not its color; popular pictures add the white.

games.q: Sam reads Kalki as pure symbol and asks you to make the best case for 'an event still ahead.' what's strongest?
o: the text itself: will be, plus a named village, a named father, a named horse.
lots of people believe it, so it has to be meant literally.
reading things as symbols is only a way to dodge hard questions.
games.why: a fair case stands on the text: bhavishyati, Shambhala, Vishnuyasha, Devadatta. Details like those are why some readers wait for an event.

practice: Bring to mind one wrong in the world you can't fix. If you pray, offer it on each breath out with words many Hindus repeat to Vishnu, Om Namo Narayanaya. If you don't pray, breathe out the words: not the last word.
Then rest with that for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Kalki: the form of Vishnu the Bhagavata says will be born at the twilight of the age, in Shambhala, riding a swift horse.

orig.note: Sanskrit bhavishyati: he will be, the verb the Bhagavata uses for Kalki.

carryVoice: For the road: God's coming isn't finished; Kalki will be. The one name in the series still written that way. Day fifteen sixty-four, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 1.3.25 (Kalki, son of Vishnuyasha, at the twilight of the age, when rulers are like robbers)
Bhagavata Purana 12.2.18–20 (born in Shambhala in Vishnuyasha's house; the horse Devadatta; the sword; the robbers who rule as kings)
Bhagavad Gita 4.7–8 (whenever dharma declines, I come forth, age after age; looked back to)
